newsitem.title: USA: Strike possibility looms at WHX Corp.
newsitem.headline: Strike possibility looms at WHX Corp.

text.p: WHX Corp, parent of Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corp, faces the possibility of a strike next week as ongoing contract talks between the company and the United Steelworkers union have been less than fruitful, union officials said.
"There's still time to resolve it, if the company wants to resolve it," said Jim Bowen, chairman of the union's negotiating committee. "But both sides are adamant on their position."
A contract covering some 4,700 steelworkers expires October 1.
Bowen said the two sides are far apart on the issue of pensions. Contract talks opened September 5 in Pittsburgh and are ongoing.

WHX has a defined contribution pension, a plan that is funded based on the number of hours an employee has worked. The union wants a defined benefit plan established, which would guarantee funding regardless of hours worked.
WHX, the ninth largest U.S. integrated steelmaker, is the only integrated steel company that does not have a defined benefit plan.
"The company is still offering defined contribution," Bowen said. "Our people have been second-class citizens in the steel industry."
Some industry sources close to the negotiations have said privately in recent weeks that the pension issue would not get resolved and a strike was almost certain.
Gregg Warren, WHX spokesman, declined to comment on negotiations. But he confirmed reports that the company offered to guarantee pensions at a minimum of $1,200 to $1,440 a month.
That offer would increase contributions for workers age 50 and older but would not include a contribution change for workers between the ages of 30 and 49.
The company's proposal also includes a signing bonus and wage increases of $0.25 per hour in 1997 and 1998.
Steel plants in West Virginia, Ohio and Pennsylvania would be affected by a strike.
